replies.author: donkeykong917
replies.body:
1. Update unreal engine to 5.8
2. Install mcp plugin insdie
3. Ask Claude to help me to connect to mcp
4. Load up car racing tutorial 
5. Install assets into project via unreal store, so maps you bought or are free
6. Ask Claude code to change the stage or cycle through what stages.
7. Boom play game.

I probably could if changed the stage myself.

Then later, need to fine tune, make menu blah blah, fine tuning will cost the tokens

replies.author: wahoozerman
replies.body:
I've been trying out 5.8 for the MCP and imo it isn't worth it. Claude is currently *very bad* at doing anything in the editor over the MCP and it requires a lot of hand holding while it burns tokens at an astonishing rate to do even basic tasks. 

I have also been using it without the MCP on a 5.7 project and it does surprisingly well. It seems like it can infer most of what is and should be in blueprints, and it will tell you what you need to hook up after it writes a bunch of C++. 

I am able to work much faster on the 5.7 project with it doing boilerplate C++ and me hooking up the end result in editor than having it do things end to end over MCP. The main advantage of the MCP though is that it can work completely autonomously while I do something like go grocery shopping. It will just burn through your whole token budget to spend an hour doing what would take you ten minutes.

replies.author: StudioNakamura
replies.body:
You don't need 5.8 to use MCP, just that 5.8 has Epic's official MCP that has a robust set of tools, but there are other MCP out there. I am on UE 5.7.4, and I am using 2 MCP, ChiR24 & Monolith. They each have their strengths and weaknesses, but it's super easy to install both, and Claude will learn on it's own, which is the best for a given task and use the correct one when appropriate. Oddly enough Opus likes Monolith best, and Fable likes ChiR24 best. Both of these run on your system without needing an external server or anything. I had Claude install and configure both. To be honest, I have had Claude do everything necessary to configure itself to work correctly. Everything. 

I am working on a very large 20K by 20K open world sandbox survival game. My world is built on Voxel Plugin 2, and because the VP2 has it's own file types, no MCP has (or had, something might now) the toolset to interface with these custom file types. like Voxel Graphs, and Voxel Height Maps. So I made Claude write his own VP2 toolset. It was simple enough to do. He looked at the VP2 source code, and probed the files and started creating the tools necessary for creating all of the voxel file types, along with being able to edit them and create all of the nodes, variables, functions, etc. To achieve this, (and yes, I frequently refer to Claude as a person, He, It, Whatever) He created a bridge that rides on top of Monolith, instead of creating a whole new MCP. He made a plugin, and adds all of the tools to this plugin. so now, this plugin could be installed, along with Monolith MCP, anywhere, and work to handle VP2 development.

Claude has been able to create anything I have asked him to create. I only ran into an issue once, with him struggling to get the dynamically generated landscape biomes blending together correctly, so I abandoned my original approach and came at it from another direction, and he nailed it easy. 

I will let you in on a little hint, when it comes to working with Claude (Or any AI) on any kind of large project. It is imperative that you give Claude a memory, and establish guard rails. If you have spent any time working with AI, you will be well accustomed to "hallucinations" ... this is because AI work on inference. They "infer" what should come next. basically making an educated guess at what they should do. You want them to do as little of this as possible. So your greatest security against this behavior, are guard rails, or rather a set of rules that Claude saves to memory (.md files) that it reads every time you start Claude up. And the #1 rule is, "Never guess about anything. Check the source code, read the documentation, and if you are still unsure, ask me what you should do." ... this alone keeps him from wasting your time building things that do not work, and ultimately rob you of hours of your life, hours of project dev time, and tokens/money spent on generation.

I won't go any deeper into this, because this response is way too long now. But suffice to say, Claude can do anything in UE that you need it to do, with very little effort, if you take the time to have it setup a set of .md files to store what it's learned, store it's "primary directives", and track current project status, its amazing how much it will help. Just give him the starting guard rails to prevent hallucinations, then tell him he is both an expert UE 5 Game Developer, and is the Project Manager for your game project, and ask him to setup project management files for the project. Then off you go. But as others have said, there is no magic AI that is going to make a AAA game for you. If you want a quality game that players will enjoy, you still need to at least know what you are doing in UE, and then you can direct Claude to do the work for you. 

Best of luck to you!

replies.author: StudioNakamura
replies.body:
I have not been using Claude for 3D Model creation, but a good friend of mine has been using it to model things in Blender, and he's had some great experience there. He hasn't been making any kind of creatures, so I don't know how well Claude would do, but I personally think you would have more luck with 3D Modeling in Blender, now that Blender has an MCP for Claude. You might give that a try. Would also be good for props. And of course Blender is free, and pretty much a must if you are working on models. I model everything myself in Blender, besides some assets I pickup from Fab. 

Then once you have an enemy model, as long as it is bipedal, try AccuRig. They have a free auto-rigging app that I find works well. and once it is rigged with AccuRig, it will import into UE and you can swap out the model in the UE5 Manny, with your imported AccuRig rigged model, and it will work as intended. I am still hunting for a good free auto-rigging app for quadrupeds. If anyone knows of one, hook me up! 😂 

Blender Download: [https://www.blender.org/download/](https://www.blender.org/download/)  
Or you can get Blender on Steam if you like, same thing and steam will auto update it. I prefer not to update my blender, and I installed through steam, then just went into the settings and disabled updates. Up to you, just giving options. 😄 

Blender MCP: [https://www.blender.org/lab/mcp-server/](https://www.blender.org/lab/mcp-server/)

AccuRig: [https://actorcore.reallusion.com/auto-rig/accurig](https://actorcore.reallusion.com/auto-rig/accurig)

Quick tutorial for rigging with AccuRig that also gives some info about generating AI characters, rigging, and importing into UE: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RFHL20AT4XA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RFHL20AT4XA)

Hope this helps.

replies.author: StudioNakamura
replies.body:
I was not sure how you were handling your character rigging, so I gave you some tips, that's all. Just trying to help if I can. Use what you need, ignore the rest. I am just sharing what I have learned from my own game dev journey. 😄 

You might have good luck with MetaHuman creator. I have not used it. I do know if you are going to use MetaHumans, you need to strip away a lot of the technical extras from the MetaHuman character for it to be performant in a full game. Just depends on the size and type of game you are making. 

From what I have read, the hair is the first thing to go, in lieu of hair cards, as the default hair is too taxing. and the second thing is face rigs that add too much weight to the characters. So for optimization, I would look at hair replacement and scrubbing the face rig from your usable game characters. You can swap in a version of the character that has the face rig if you are doing a close up cut scene, then swap back to the scrubbed character for gameplay. That's the extent of my knowledge on MetaHumans. All "human" characters in my game are built on custom models and I have no need for MetaHuman.

You should have good luck with Blender and props. As for clothing for MetaHumans, like a robe, it probably needs to be skeletal mesh carrying the same MetaHuman skeleton, or be weight painted to the MetaHuman skeleton to bend and follow the body correctly with minimal clipping. Hopefully the Blender MCP for Claude will help.
